Forms are heavily used in SaaS applications, whether it be for an onboarding experience,
submitting an email, or filling out your account settings like the example we're going

to go with it.

to receive.

Now, when you are working with long forms like this, it can be a bit overwhelming

One way to make forms, a little more digestible, is to group related fields together
to help the user make sense of all the information.

Now, there's not necessarily anything wrong with that, but a great way to deal with this

By increasing the height of the inputs, we give everything more room to breathe,
making the form easier to digest.

And while we're focused on these inputs, we're also going to go ahead and update the drop-down
arrow icons to something a little more modern.
This may seem like an insignificant change, but it's many small changes like this
that are going to make a big difference in the end.
Okay, let's talk about the space between these form elements.
I see this happening way too often in the form design, and that is when the label for
the input will blow it is too close to the input above it.
Not only does it make things confusing, but it also looks crammed in unprofessional.

To fix this, increase the margin below each input, so it's clear which label
belongs to which input.
Okay, let's take a look at these buttons.
When there are multiple actions, a user can take on a page,
it's easy to fall into the trap of designing those actions based purely on
semantics.
The thinking goes something like this.
If it's a positive action, make the button blue or green.
If it's a high severity action, make the button red.
Now, of course, semantics are important, but more importantly, you need to consider the
hierarchy in these situations.

Finally, let's make some adjustments to these workflow buttons.
